metadata.description: Low-level bindings to the system libz library (also known as zlib).

classification.reasoning: Purpose: `libz-sys` is a well-known, foundational, low-level binding crate to the zlib/zlib-ng compression library with hundreds of millions of downloads and an age of over 4,000 days. Sources: build.rs reads standard environment variables (`HOST`, `TARGET`, `OUT_DIR`) and checks features/`LIBZ_SYS_STATIC` to configure compilation. Sinks/Flows: files are written to OUT_DIR as part of native library compilation (`fs::write`), and `std::process::Command` is used in `zng/cc.rs` to invoke a C compiler (`cfg.get_compiler().path()`), which is standard behavior for native sys crates. Anomalies: none. The raw flagged signals (file_write, env_var_read, process_spawn) are entirely consistent with legitimate native build scripts compiling C libraries (supported by benign false positive patterns). Conclusion: benign, trusted crate.

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: legitimate build.rs signals that are NOT malicious
retrieved_context.text: Common benign reasons a crate's build.rs may trigger a raw signal match: checking the installed rustc/cargo version via Command::new (used by serde and many other major crates to gate feature availability); generating code from a schema or protobuf definition, sometimes fetched over network from a first-party, well-known source; reading a small number of standard, non-sensitive environment variables like OUT_DIR, TARGET, or CARGO_PKG_VERSION which Cargo itself sets. A high-quality classifier should not flag these alone -- context (destination of network calls, sensitivity of specific env var names read, and the crate's stated purpose) matters more than raw signal presence.
retrieved_context.source: synthesized from observed benign build.rs behavior, e.g. serde

retrieved_context.title: TrapDoor campaign (May 2026)
retrieved_context.text: A cross-ecosystem attack campaign using build.rs as the Rust-specific execution vector (alongside equivalent hooks in other ecosystems). Demonstrated that the build.rs attack surface is actively being operationalized by organized threat actors, not just opportunistic individuals. Attack category: build.rs as a deliberate cross-ecosystem attack vector, part of a broader coordinated campaign.

retrieved_context.title: logs-update: credential and file stealer in library code, no build script (September 2026)
retrieved_context.text: A crate published on 2026-09-10 that presents itself as a terminal progress-bar library but renders nothing. It has NO build script, so it does not run during `cargo build` of a dependent; it runs when its binary is executed (for example after `cargo install`) or when a dependent calls its run() function. It POSTs a machine fingerprint (username, OS, local IP) to an attacker web endpoint; reads the project's .env and trading-bot config files and POSTs them; walks the filesystem and POSTs the contents of .env, .json, .txt, .doc/.docx and .xlsx files; and on Linux appends an attacker's SSH public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for remote login. It targets crypto trading-bot developers. Reported as malicious in every version. Lesson: a build-script-only detector sees nothing here; the tell-tale combination is network POSTs plus filesystem walking plus credential-file paths in library code.
